rows.subtopic: Menstrual cycle effects on mood and coping
rows.description: A respectful partner asks how she is feeling instead of blaming every mood on her cycle. Experiences differ hugely between people, and dismissing real concerns as hormones is unfair and shuts down honest talk.

rows.subtopic: Menstrual cycle effects on mood and coping
rows.description: When mood or pain around periods becomes overwhelming, disrupts work or relationships, or brings very dark thoughts, it deserves a doctor's attention. Being taken seriously, not told to tolerate it, is a right.

rows.subtype: Body tension and slump as signals [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler stiffens with anger, goes limp in a tantrum or leans against a parent when tired. These are mostly body states rather than planned messages; a calm adult reads them as need for rest, comfort or help.

A child hunches, tucks in the chin or curls up on a sofa after being scolded or teased. It can signal sadness, shame or a wish to hide; a quiet, non-intrusive presence works better than asking many questions.
A young adult stiffens, holds the breath or hunches in a stressful exam or confrontation. It signals threat or anxiety; slow exhaling, dropping the shoulders and grounding the feet often ease it.
A child learns to hold back interruptions, raise a hand and wait for a pause. Norms vary: in some families overlapping talk shows warmth and interest, in others it seems disrespectful.
A young adult in negotiation or interview may use a brief pause to think or let a point land. A long silence can feel like pressure in some cultures and respect in others, so the setting guides use.

In many Indian homes a child learns that respect for elders and modesty matter, so opinions are held back at home while voiced freely with friends. Personality is shown differently in different rooms.
A boy told not to cry hides sadness and a girl told to be quiet hides ambition. Learned rules shape which traits feel safe, and adults who widen the range help teenagers become fuller selves.
An eldest sibling grows into a responsible, serious role, caring for parents and younger ones and delaying own wants. Duty becomes identity, and sometimes hides tiredness and a wish for freedom.

rows.subtype: Playing a role until it takes over [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager given the role of prefect or gang lookout begins to act tougher than they are, and in time the behaviour feels natural. The costume of the role slowly changes what they think is acceptable.

Seniors in a hostel or student volunteers enforce rules harshly on juniors because the role licenses it, and they come to believe the juniors deserve it. Roles, uniforms and few checks can bring out cruelty in ordinary people.
A teenager delivers a joke or an insult without expression, so listeners cannot tell if it is humour. Deadpan needs shared understanding, and unclear cases are settled by asking.

rows.subtype: Deadpan and impassive as professional style [Mismatch]
rows.description: A young adult in a serious workplace keeps a blank, even manner. It can signal composure, disinterest or hidden strain, so meaning comes from patterns and direct conversation.
